newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-Will Bonn hit its deficit goal? - by W.Hess.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Will Bonn hit its deficit goal? - by W.Hess.

text.p: By Werner Hess, Economist at the Dresdner Bank, Frankfurt
The government working group on taxes last week forecast a tax revenue shortfall of 18 billion marks. The German government itself has only limited influence on the total public budget balance.

Firstly, the balance also reflects the influences of the overall economic climate, which cannot be directly attributed to financial policy. Secondly, the central government is not the only cause of the public deficit. Nevertheless, we believe that doubts that monetary union will start on time because of the estimated tax revenue shortfall are inappropriate.

For its budgetary planning at the beginning of the year, the German government assumed nominal GDP growth of 3.5 percent, an increase in tax income of 3 percent and average unemployment of 4.1 million. Under these conditions, the government estimated the public budget deficit at 105 billion marks or at 2.9 percent of GDP.

While our assessments show the economy to be living up to expectations, this is not the case for the other two assumptions: According to the new tax estimates the tax income in 1997 will only increase by about 1.5 percent; even the government now estimates the number of unemployed at 4.3 million.

100,000 additional unemployed lead to extra expenses for the state. Unemployment and social benefits of roughly 2.2 billion marks and a shortfall in social security contributions of 0.9 billion marks thus burden the overall public budget with a substantial three billion marks.

At first glance, together with the estimated tax revenue shortfall of 18 billion marks, that makes a budget deficit 24 billion marks higher than had been planned up to now; with this figure the deficit would be at 3.5 percent of GDP.
However, it must also be considered that since the tax estimate last autumn, many figures in the budgetary plan have shifted -- not all to the disadvantage of the financial situation.

Firstly, according to our estimates, government expenditure on goods and services will only moderately increase by a nominal one percent. The reduction in public service workers, the low wage increases and the reforms in statutory health insurance particularly help to curb the increase here.

Secondly, the interest expenses will be significantly lower than originally expected. One reason is the decreased interest rates level, and another is that debt management is increasingly choosing loan forms that allow the interest to be paid in the future.

Thirdly, the increase in the social security contribution rates -- as questionable as that may be for growth prospects -- leads to a reversal from last year's deficit to a surplus this year. Fourthly, there could once again be positive surprises in the tax revenue during the year.

The lower tax revenues at the beginning of this year are distorted by a series of special effects, including an unusually low number of working days, which has significantly forced down real net output and sales. Therefore, all in all a consolidation in the government's budget of 10 billion marks at the most is currently needed to meet the deficit reference value of the Maastricht treaty.

To qualify that, it is important to note that tax revenue estimates are anything but reliable. In addition to economic development, tax revenues depend on many mainly structural factors, which can correct the economic influences.

The connection between revenue and the tax base has also relaxed because in the face of a high tax burden, tax payers increasingly look for alternatives or take advantage of tax privileges and possibilities to shape transactions in order to achieve the most favourable tax result. Against this background and with a view to the development of unemployment, budget deficit forecasts are extremely uncertain.

Cuts in spending to compensate for the shortfalls are imperative. In addition to that, the efforts of financial policy are obviously directed at taking the heat out of the budget situation using purely technical changes in the balance sheet.

If or to what extent the higher evaluation of the Bundesbank gold reserves currently being considered would reduce the deficit is, however, still disputed among experts. As sensible as this revaluation seems viewed systematically, the current discussion surrounding it is problematic, which set against the background of tax revenue shortfalls gives the impression of "creative accounting".

Even if consolidation is carried out by increasing indirect taxes, the loss of credibility for financial policy would be immense. In the present situation it seems absurd to thwart plans for cuts in income and corporate tax with a tax increase, the only purpose of which is to fill budget gaps.

Due to weak domestic demand, this would frankly be poison for the widely export driven upturn in the economy. Consolidation must take place exclusively on the expenditure side. Subsidies among other things offer plenty of room to manoeuvre here.
